title: Student Health Insurance
difficulty_source_label: Overall 2, Quant 2, Creativity 3 (1-3 scale); Quant Level - MEDIUM
fit_question: When did you make a lasting impact on a team? Alternatively, what would your last manager say is a reason not to hire you?
prompt: A business unit of a national health insurer sells medical, prescription-drug, and dental insurance to students at large universities. It leads the market with about 500,000 customers and $500M revenue in a 2.5M-customer, $2.2B potential market. Sales require winning a campus health center and then students, sometimes through a broker. Operating margin has fallen from 25% five years ago to 9%, competition is aggressive, budgets are shrinking, students through age 26 may remain on parents' plans, and insurers must spend 80% of revenue on medical expenses. Identify and prioritize profitable growth opportunities for the next three years.
interviewer_notes: Run the six questions sequentially as mini-cases; do not request a traditional framework. The case tests structured brainstorming and synthesis across dense exhibits. Growth options include the core market, small schools, new products, and new business models. Before providing Data Sheet 2, require the candidate to identify inputs needed for operating margin. None of the four small-school scenarios reaches the current 9% margin, so a different cost structure or direct-to-student model is required.

suggested_framework.summary: Generate growth options across current and new customers and products, then prioritize on strategic impact, economics, required investment, and feasibility.

children.label: Improve pricing, sales, differentiation, and large-school share
Small colleges, secondary schools, uninsured students, and direct sales
Tuition, electronics, auto, renters, mental-health, wellness, billing, and digital care
Market size, margin, fit, investment, capability, complexity, and partners

stages.interviewer_asks: What potential growth avenues should the student-health business consider?
stages.expected_answer: Defend and grow large schools through pricing, sales effectiveness, and differentiation; enter small schools, secondary schools, or reach students directly; sell adjacent insurance such as tuition, electronics, auto, and renters; add mental-health, wellness, billing, or remote-care services; and design stripped-down coverage for cost-conscious uninsured students.
good_answer_signals: Uses existing/new product and customer buckets
Covers both institutional and student purchasers

stages.interviewer_asks: What trends in Data Sheet 1 suggest growth opportunities?
stages.expected_answer: Schools below 10,000 students contain 42% of students and nearly 90% of schools, yet large schools generate 93% of client revenue, indicating small-school white space and concentration risk. Medical insurance provides 99% of product revenue, while dental, discount cards, and student assistance total only 1%. Low school and student penetration of ancillary products suggests meaningful cross-sell opportunity.
good_answer_signals: Combines school distribution with revenue concentration
Identifies both small-school and cross-sell opportunities
Avoids treating white space as automatically profitable

stages.interviewer_asks: What criteria should the client use to assess the small-school market?
stages.expected_answer: Quantify schools, students, insurance requirements, premiums, growth, share, win rates, margin scenarios, investment, and sensitivity. Qualitatively assess buying behavior, reform trends, competition, strategic fit, required capabilities, customer needs, cost versus differentiation, and likely penetration. Use interviews, focus groups, competitor research, and capability-gap analysis.
good_answer_signals: Covers size, growth, competition, fit, capabilities, profitability, and penetration
Links entry attractiveness to operating model

stages.interviewer_asks: Using Data Sheet 2, calculate operating margin for each product and customer scenario.
stages.release_when: Provide Data Sheet 2 only after the candidate requests price, students per school, medical and selling expense, setup cost, and administration cost.
stages.expected_answer: Option A, Plus at a large school: 500 students and $945K cost on $1M revenue, giving 5.5%. B, Standard large: 1,000 students and $970K cost, giving 3.0%. C, Plus small: 250 students and $497.5K cost on $500K, giving 0.5%. D, Standard small: 500 students and $510K cost, giving -2.0%. Larger customers absorb fixed setup cost better, and Plus halves per-student administration cost because the same premium revenue comes from half as many students.
good_answer_signals: Derives student counts from premium revenue and price
Treats setup as fixed per school

stages.interviewer_asks: Should the client pursue small schools, and under what model?
stages.expected_answer: Do not use the current model unchanged: even the best 5.5% scenario is below the business's 9% margin. Price increases and lower medical spending are constrained by reform, so reduce selling, setup, and administrative cost through process redesign and contract changes. The strongest option is an online direct-to-student model that bypasses schools and brokers, subject to acquisition-cost, compliance, service, and conversion tests.

stages.interviewer_asks: How would you prioritize core share, small schools, and new products?
stages.expected_answer: Score each on strategic differentiation and unmet need; revenue, margin, cost avoidance, and downside; capital and operating investment; and implementation complexity, capabilities, and partner availability. Protect the profitable core first, pursue ancillary-product cross-sell because the base is underpenetrated, and pilot direct-to-student small-school entry only if it can exceed the 9% margin. Sequence larger or more disruptive bets behind evidence from pilots.
good_answer_signals: Uses case evidence to sequence opportunities

exhibits.title: Student health market and product penetration
exhibits.description: Four charts show school-size distribution, revenue by school size, product revenue contribution, and school/student penetration of ancillary products.
exhibits.key_insight: Revenue is concentrated in large schools and medical insurance despite substantial small-school and ancillary-product white space.

exhibits.title: Historical financials and small-school scenario inputs
exhibits.description: Historical revenue and pretax operating income plus product price, school revenue, and cost assumptions for four customer-product scenarios.
exhibits.key_insight: The fixed per-school setup cost and per-student administration burden make smaller and lower-priced accounts structurally less profitable.

math.question: What is operating margin in the four product/customer scenarios?

synthesis: Prioritize defending the large-school core and cross-selling underpenetrated ancillary products. Do not enter small schools with the current two-stage model: all four scenarios fall below the current 9% margin. Pilot a direct online student model that removes intermediaries and lowers selling, setup, and administration cost, then scale only if unit economics, compliance, service, and acquisition performance clear the margin threshold.
what_great_looks_like: Extracts combined insights from multiple charts
Proposes and prioritizes a direct business model
common_pitfalls: Assuming small-school white space is profitable
Treating setup cost as variable per student
Suggesting lower medical cost despite the 80% requirement

extraction.notes: All four margin scenarios were independently recomputed and match the source. Option C total cost is exactly $497.5K; the source displays the rounded $498K while retaining the correct 0.5% margin. Reviewed and accepted by Claude 2026-09-30.
